_comment: AGENT TOPOLOGY — this file is DOCUMENTATION, not OpenClaw config.
It was originally written as a mergeable openclaw.json fragment. That was
wrong: it described a schema that does not exist in OpenClaw 2026.7.1-2.
The real schema was read on 2026-09-08 (`openclaw config schema`) and the
differences were not cosmetic:
* There is no `agents.<name>.tools`. Tool policy is GLOBAL only —
tools.profile / tools.allow / tools.deny / tools.byProvider. Per-agent
tool lists are not a thing this version supports.
* Per-agent entries live in `agents.list` (an array), and skills attach
via `agents.defaults.skills`.
* Model providers take `api`, not `type`. The lmstudio plugin already
advertises `text-inference: lmstudio` as a capability.
* There is no `scheduling` key. Scheduled work is `cron`, and jobs live
in cron.store, managed by CLI rather than config.
The applied config is ops/phase6a.patch.json5. This file records the
INTENT — which agent does what, and why each one has nothing — so the
reasoning survives even though the shape changed.
Kept as JSON so tests can assert against it.
_how_the_zero_tool_guarantee_is_actually: Not per-agent, as originally designed. Globally, in three layers:
tools.deny    = [bash,...] blocks named tools regardless of the above
Global turns out to be STRONGER than what was intended. A per-agent list
protects the agents someone remembered to configure. An empty global
allowlist covers every agent, including ones a future update introduces.
Under D-009 the LMS runs as Matthew's own macOS user, so an injected agent
would inherit his Messages, iCloud and Keychain. There is no privilege
boundary underneath. This is what replaces it: agents read text and return
text; every effect is deterministic Python in core/, invoked by launchd.

lms-orchestrator._role: Returns the name of the next pipeline step from a fixed enum. core/ validates the name and runs the function. A name outside the enum is a hard error, so the worst case is an artifact in the wrong queue where a human sees it.

lms-classifier._role: The only component that reads untrusted content. Constrained decoding means it cannot emit anything but the schema.

lms-drafter._role: Writes reply text. No mailbox, no network, no send. core/ puts the text in Gmail drafts; a Telegram tap is what sends it.

_comment: Tier names are normative; model names are not. Substitute the current
MLX build — re-benchmarking is a quarterly ops item, not a build blocker.
No cloud tier (D-003). The spec's cloud guards are NOT built:
block_cloud_if_tax_engagement, block_cloud_if_unredacted_pii,
reason-code gating, DEC-3/DEC-10. The absence of an API key is not the
control — the absence of those guards is the reason there is no key.

lmstudio._verified: lsof shows 127.0.0.1:1234, not *:1234. 'Serve on Local Network' stays off.

TIER-OCR._comment: Apple Vision first; this is the low-confidence fallback.

_comment: INTENT ONLY. The live key is `cron`, and jobs are managed by the CLI,
not by this file. Recorded here so the intended times and the DST
reasoning are in one place.
America/New_York as a NAMED ZONE, never a UTC offset (Rec 21). An
offset is correct for half the year and silently an hour wrong for the
other half — the brief simply starts arriving at 05:30 from November
and nobody connects it to a config value.
verify_setup.py check 4 asserts the local hour holds across the
November boundary.
ownerAllowFrom is EMPTY and that is a live gap, not a placeholder.
`openclaw doctor` says so: 'No command owner is configured.' Until a
numeric Telegram id lands here, /halt — the sole remote kill switch
(D-005) — has no authorised sender, and `security audit --deep` keeps
reporting 'gateway.probe_failed / missing scope: operator.read'.
Those two findings are the same finding. Filled in Phase 7 from the id
on Matthew's first message to the bot. Numeric id, never the @handle:
the Bot API only reports the numeric id, and handles can change.
